phase1.intro:
Sometimes order doesn't matter and duplicates are actively wrong — that's what Set is for.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What's the whole point of a Set?
dialogue: [[key:Membership is the entire point, and every element appears at most once]], no matter how many times you try to add it again — a guest list, a set of tags.

stickyNote.flavor: 1️⃣ every element appears at most once
stickyNote.definition: A Set guarantees no duplicates — membership (is this here?) is the whole point, not order or position.

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between HashSet and TreeSet?
dialogue: [[term:HashSet]] is the default choice — backed by a hash table, O(1) average for add()/contains()/remove(). [[warn:Never write code that depends on HashSet's iteration order]] — it's an implementation detail, not a promise.
[[term:TreeSet]] trades that speed for structure — sorted order at all times, O(log n), but gives you `first()`, `last()`, `lower()`, `higher()` for free.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚡ O(1) unordered vs. O(log n) always sorted
stickyNote.definition: HashSet: O(1) average, no order guarantee. TreeSet: O(log n), always sorted, with first()/last()/lower()/higher() lookups.

topics.buttonText: Why does a custom object need equals() and hashCode() to work in a Set?
dialogue: A HashSet only knows two Person objects are "the same" if `equals()` and `hashCode()` say so. Without overriding both, every new Person() looks unique to the set, even with identical fields. [[fun:This is exactly why every class that might end up in a Set or as a Map key needs its own equals()/hashCode() pair]].

stickyNote.definition: A Set relies on equals() and hashCode() to detect duplicates. A custom class without both looks unique every time, even with identical data.

mcq.question:
You need to store a growing list of usernames, guarantee no duplicates, and you'll frequently need them printed alphabetically for a report. Which is the single best fit?

A) ArrayList, sorting manually before each report
B) HashSet — fastest add/contains, order doesn't matter here anyway
C) TreeSet — no duplicates AND always sorted, no manual sort step needed
D) LinkedList, since it preserves insertion order

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Creates an ArrayList<Integer> with numbers: [1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1, 6]
2. Creates a HashSet<Integer> from the list (removing duplicates)
3. Prints the HashSet
4. Creates a TreeSet<Integer> from the same list
5. Prints the TreeSet (should be sorted)
6. Prints the size of both sets
7. Checks if both sets contain the number 4

phase5.trivia: HashSet is actually built on top of HashMap internally — every element you add becomes a key in a hidden HashMap, mapped to a shared dummy placeholder value. That's why HashSet and HashMap share the same O(1) average-case performance and the same equals()/hashCode() requirement.
